items.name: Definition 2.2
items.statement:
Given $C \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, open and convex, and $d \in \mathcal{D}(C)$, a function $H: \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}_+ \cup \{+\infty\}$ is called the induced proximal distance to $d$ if $H$ is finite valued on $C \times C$ and for each $a, b \in C$ satisfies

$$
H (a, a) = 0, \tag {2.5}
$$

$$
\langle c - b, \nabla_ {1} d (b, a) \rangle \leq H (c, a) - H (c, b) \quad \forall c \in C. \tag {2.6}
$$

We write $(d,H)\in \mathcal{F}(C)$ to quantify the triple $[C,d,H]$ that satisfies the premises of Definition 2.2.

Likewise, we will write $(d,H)\in \mathcal{F}(\overline{C})$ for the triple $[\overline{C},d,H]$ whenever there exists $H$ which is finite valued on $\overline{C}\times C$, satisfies (2.5)-(2.6) for any $c\in \overline{C}$, and is such that $\forall c\in \overline{C}$ one has $H(c,\cdot)$ level bounded on $C$. Clearly, one has $\mathcal{F}(\overline{C})\subset \mathcal{F}(C)$.

The motivation behind such a construction is not as mysterious as it might look at first sight. Indeed, for the moment, notice that the classical PA, which corresponds to the special case $C = \overline{C} = \mathbb{R}^n$, $d(x,y) = 2^{-1}\| x - y\|^2$ and the induced proximal distance $H$ being exactly $d$, clearly satisfies (2.6), thanks to the well-known identity

$$
\| z - x \| ^ {2} = \| z - y \| ^ {2} + \| y - x \| ^ {2} + 2 \langle z - y, y - x \rangle .
$$

To handle the constraint cases C versus $\overline{C}$, we consider two types of kernels h. The first type consists of convex kernel functions h (often called a Bregman function with zone C; see, e.g., [15]) that satisfy the following conditions:

$(B_{1})$ dom h = $\overline{C}$ ;  
$(B_{2})$ (i) $\forall x \in \overline{C}, D_{h}(x, \cdot)$ is level bounded on int(dom h);  
(ii) $\forall y \in C, D_{h}(\cdot, y)$ is level bounded;  
$(B_{3})$ $\forall y\in \mathrm{dom}h,\forall \{y_k\} \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathrm{dom}h)$ with $\lim_{k\to \infty}y_k = y$, one has $\lim_{k\to \infty}$ $D_{h}(y,y_{k}) = 0;$

3.2. Self-proximal methods. The three point identity (3.2) plays a fundamental role in the convergence of Bregman-based self-proximal methods, namely those for which we take $d$ itself as a Bregman proximal distance, that is, $d(x,y) = H(x,y) = D_h(x,y)$, with $D_h$ as defined in (3.1). Whenever $h \in \mathcal{B}$, or in $\mathcal{WB}$, properties $(P_1)$, $(P_2)$, and $(P_3)$ hold for $d = D_h$.

Clearly, $D_h(a, a) = 0 \quad \forall a \in C$ , so that $(P_4)$ holds, and since $H$ is always nonnegative it follows (3.2) that (2.6) holds. Therefore for $h \in \mathcal{WB}$ one has $(d, H) = (D_h, D_h) \in \mathcal{F}(C)$ , while if $h \in \mathcal{B}$ , then $(d, H) = (D_h, D_h) \in \mathcal{F}_+(\overline{C})$ .

When $C = \mathbb{R}^n$, with $h(\cdot) = \| \cdot \|^2 / 2 \in \mathcal{B}$, then $D_h(x, y) = \| x - y \|^2 / 2$, and with $(d, H) = (D_h, D_h) \in \mathcal{F}_+(\mathbb{R}^n)$, the IPA is exactly the classical proximal method and Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 cover the usual convergence results, e.g., [24, 30, 31].

4. Interior gradient methods. When $\overline{C} = R^{n}$, Correa and Lemarechal [17] and Robinson [38] have remarked that the PA can be viewed as an $\epsilon$ -subgradient descent method. This idea was recently extended by Auslender and Teboulle [7] for the logarithmic-quadratic proximal method which allows us to handle linear inequality constraints directly. Given the framework developed in section 2, we extend these results for more general constraints and with various classes of proximal distances.

We first give the main convergence result. We then present applications and examples which allow us to improve some known interior gradient-based methods as well as to derive new and simple convergent algorithms for conic optimization problems.

5. Interior gradient methods with improved efficiency. In this section, we further analyze the global convergence rate of interior gradient methods, and we propose a new interior scheme which improves their efficiency. The classical gradient method for minimizing a continuously differentiable function over $R^{n}$ with Lipschitz gradient is known to exhibit an $O(k^{-1})$ global convergence rate estimate for function values. In [34], Nesterov developed what he called an “optimal algorithm” for smooth convex minimization and was able to improve the efficiency of the gradient method

by constructing a method that keeps the simplicity of the gradient method but with the faster rate $O(k^{-2})$. Inspired by this work, it is thus natural to ask if this kind of result can be extended to interior gradient methods. We answer this question positively for a class of interior gradient methods. We propose an algorithm that provides a natural extension of the results of [34] and leads to a simple “optimal” interior gradient method for convex conic problems.

Consider the conic optimization problem as described in section 4.2.1, i.e.,

$$
\inf \{f (x): x \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V} \},
q _ {k + 1} (x) - f (x) \leq (1 - \alpha_ {k}) (q _ {k} (x) - f (x)) \quad \forall x \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V}.
q _ {k} (x) - f (x) \leq \gamma_ {k} (q _ {0} (x) - f (x)) \quad \forall x \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V},
\gamma_ {k} := \prod_ {l = 0} ^ {k - 1} (1 - \alpha_ {l}).

f (x ^ {k}) \leq \min _ {z \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V}} q _ {k} (z) := q _ {k} ^ {*}.
$$

We begin by constructing the sequence of functions $\{q_k(\cdot)\}$. For that purpose, we take here $d \equiv H \in \mathcal{D}(C)$, where $H$ is a Bregman proximal distance (cf. (3.1)) with kernel $h$ such that

(h1) $\operatorname{dom} h = \overline{C}$,  
(h2) $h$ is $\sigma$ -strongly convex on $C \cap \mathcal{V}$.

For every $k \geq 0$ and for any $x \in \overline{C} \cap V$, we construct the sequence $\{q_{k}(x)\}$ recursively via

$$

l _ {k} (x, y ^ {k}) = f (y ^ {k}) + \langle x - y ^ {k}, \nabla f (y ^ {k}) \rangle .

z ^ {k} = \underset {x \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V}} {\operatorname{argmin}} q _ {k} (x), q _ {k} ^ {*} = q _ {k} (z ^ {k}), c _ {0} = c, z ^ {0} = x ^ {0} \in C \cap \mathcal {V}. \tag {5.10}
$$

Furthermore, the sequence $\{z^k\} \in C\cap \mathcal{V}$ is uniquely defined by

(5.11)

$$
z ^ {k + 1} = \operatorname{argmin} \left\{\left\langle x, \frac {\alpha_ {k}}{c _ {k + 1}} \nabla f (y ^ {k}) \right\rangle + H (x, z ^ {k}) \Big | x \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V} \right\} \equiv u \left(\frac {\alpha_ {k}}{c _ {k + 1}} \nabla f (y ^ {k}), z ^ {k}\right),
$$

where the positive sequence $\{c_k\}$ satisfies $c_{k + 1} = (1 - \alpha_k)c_k$.

z ^ {k + 1} = \operatorname{argmin} \left\{\left\langle x, \frac {\alpha_ {k}}{c _ {k + 1}} \nabla f (y ^ {k}) \right\rangle + H (x, z ^ {k}) \Big | x \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V} \right\} \equiv u \left(\frac {\alpha_ {k}}{c _ {k + 1}} \nabla f (y ^ {k}), z ^ {k}\right),
q _ {k} (x) = q _ {k} ^ {*} + c _ {k} H (x, z ^ {k}) \quad \forall x \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V}
z ^ {k} = \underset {x \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V}} {\operatorname{argmin}} q _ {k} (x), q _ {k} ^ {*} = q _ {k} (z ^ {k}), c _ {0} = c, z ^ {0} = x ^ {0} \in C \cap \mathcal {V}.

z ^ {k + 1} = \operatorname{argmin} \left\{\left\langle x, \frac {\alpha_ {k}}{c _ {k + 1}} \nabla f (y ^ {k}) \right\rangle + H (x, z ^ {k}) \Big | x \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V} \right\} \equiv u \left(\frac {\alpha_ {k}}{c _ {k + 1}} \nabla f (y ^ {k}), z ^ {k}\right),
$$

where the positive sequence $\{c_k\}$ satisfies $c_{k + 1} = (1 - \alpha_k)c_k$.

Proof. The proof is by induction and will use key identity (3.2). For $k = 0$, since $z^0 = x^0$ by (5.5), one has $q_0(x) = f(x^0) + cH(x,z^0)$. Then since $c\nabla_1H(z^0,z^0) = 0$ (recall the properties of $H$ ), and since $z_0 \in C \cap \mathcal{V}$, the optimality conditions imply that $z^0 = \operatorname{argmin}_{x \in \overline{C} \cap \mathcal{V}} q_0(x)$. Now suppose that (5.9) holds for some $k$ and let us prove that for any $x \in \overline{C} \cap \mathcal{V}$,

$$
q _ {k + 1} (x) = q _ {k + 1} ^ {*} + c _ {k + 1} H (x, z ^ {k + 1}).

z ^ {k + 1} = \underset {x \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V}} {\operatorname{argmin}} q _ {k + 1} (x) = u \left(\frac {\alpha_ {k}}{c _ {k + 1}} \nabla f (y ^ {k}), z ^ {k}\right)
$$

with $z^{k + 1}\in C\cap \mathcal{V}$, and

$$
q _ {k + 1} ^ {*} = q _ {k + 1} (z ^ {k + 1}) = (1 - \alpha_ {k}) q _ {k} ^ {*} + c _ {k + 1} H (z ^ {k + 1}, z ^ {k}) + \alpha_ {k} l _ {k} (z ^ {k + 1}, y ^ {k}).

c _ {k + 1} \langle \nabla_ {1} H (z ^ {k + 1}, z ^ {k}), z ^ {k + 1} - x \rangle = - \langle \alpha_ {k} \nabla f (y ^ {k}), z ^ {k + 1} - x \rangle \quad \forall x \in \overline {{C}} \cap \mathcal {V}.

items.name: Theorem 5.1
items.statement:
Let $\sigma > 0$, $L > 0$ be given. Suppose that for some $k \geq 0$ we have a point $x^k \in C \cap \mathcal{V}$ such that $f(x^k) \leq q_k^* = \min\{q_k(x) : x \in \overline{C} \cap \mathcal{V}\}$. Let $\alpha_k \in [0,1)$, $c_{k+1} = (1 - \alpha_k)c_k$, and $C \cap \mathcal{V} \ni \{z^k\}$ be given by (5.11). Define

$$
y ^ {k} = (1 - \alpha_ {k}) x ^ {k} + \alpha_ {k} z ^ {k}, \tag {5.18}
$$

$$
x ^ {k + 1} = (1 - \alpha_ {k}) x ^ {k} + \alpha_ {k} z ^ {k + 1}. \tag {5.19}
$$

Then, the following inequality holds:

$$
q _ {k + 1} ^ {*} \geq f (x ^ {k + 1}) + \frac {1}{2} \left(\frac {c _ {k + 1} \sigma}{\alpha_ {k} ^ {2}} - L\right) \| x ^ {k + 1} - y ^ {k} \| ^ {2}.
$$
formulas: y ^ {k} = (1 - \alpha_ {k}) x ^ {k} + \alpha_ {k} z ^ {k},

q _ {k + 1} ^ {*} \geq f (x ^ {k + 1}) + \frac {1}{2} \left(\frac {c _ {k + 1} \sigma}{\alpha_ {k} ^ {2}} - L\right) \| x ^ {k + 1} - y ^ {k} \| ^ {2}.
$$

Proof. Let $x \in \overline{C} \cap \mathcal{V}$. Since $q_k(x) = q_k^* + c_k H(x, z^k)$, then by (5.6) and using $c_{k+1} = (1 - \alpha_k)c_k$ one has

$$
q _ {k + 1} (x) = (1 - \alpha_ {k}) q _ {k} ^ {*} + c _ {k + 1} H (x, z ^ {k}) + \alpha_ {k} l _ {k} (x, y ^ {k}),
$$

and with $z^{k + 1} = \operatorname{argmin}_{x\in \overline{C}\cap \mathcal{V}}q_{k + 1}(x)$ one obtains

$$
q _ {k + 1} (z ^ {k + 1}) = q _ {k + 1} ^ {*} = (1 - \alpha_ {k}) q _ {k} ^ {*} + c _ {k + 1} H (z ^ {k + 1}, z ^ {k}) + \alpha_ {k} l _ {k} (z ^ {k + 1}, y ^ {k}).

q _ {k} ^ {*} \geq f (x ^ {k}) \geq f (y ^ {k}) + \langle x ^ {k} - y ^ {k}, \nabla f (y ^ {k}) \rangle ,
$$

and it follows from (5.20) and (5.7) that

$$
q _ {k + 1} ^ {*} \geq f (y ^ {k}) + c _ {k + 1} H (z ^ {k + 1}, z ^ {k}) + \langle \nabla f (y ^ {k}), r ^ {k} \rangle ,

r ^ {k} = (1 - \alpha_ {k}) x ^ {k} + \alpha_ {k} z ^ {k} - y ^ {k} + \alpha_ {k} (z ^ {k + 1} - z ^ {k}),
$$

and since by definition one has $(1 - \alpha_{k})x^{k} + \alpha_{k}z^{k} - y^{k} = 0$, then (5.21) reduces to

$$
q _ {k + 1} ^ {*} \geq f (y ^ {k}) + c _ {k + 1} H (z ^ {k + 1}, z ^ {k}) + \langle \alpha_ {k} (z ^ {k + 1} - z ^ {k}), \nabla f (y ^ {k}) \rangle .
q _ {k + 1} ^ {*} \geq f (y ^ {k}) + \frac {1}{2} \frac {c _ {k + 1} \sigma}{\alpha_ {k} ^ {2}} \| x ^ {k + 1} - y ^ {k} \| ^ {2} + \langle \nabla f (y ^ {k}), x ^ {k + 1} - y ^ {k} \rangle .
f (y ^ {k}) + \langle x ^ {k + 1} - y ^ {k}, \nabla f (y ^ {k}) \rangle \geq f (x ^ {k + 1}) - \frac {L}{2} \| x ^ {k + 1} - y ^ {k} \| ^ {2}.

items.name: Lemma 5.3
items.statement:
Let $\lambda_k > 0$, $c_k > 0$ with $c_0 = c$, and let $\{\alpha_k\}$ be the sequence with $\alpha_k \in [0,1[$ defined by $\alpha_k^2 = \lambda_k c_k(1 - \alpha_k)$ with $c_{k+1} = (1 - \alpha_k)c_k$. Set $\gamma_k := \prod_{l=0}^{k-1}(1 - \alpha_l)$. Then

$$
\gamma_ {k} \leq \left(1 + \frac {\sqrt {c}}{2} \sum_ {l = 0} ^ {k - 1} \sqrt {\lambda_ {l}}\right) ^ {- 2}.
$$

In particular, with $\lambda_{l} = \lambda$ $\forall l$ we have $\gamma_{k}\leq 4(k\sqrt{\lambda c} +2)^{-2}$.

We thus obtain a convergent interior gradient method with an improved convergence rate estimate.

items.name: Theorem 5.2
items.latex: f (x ^ {k}) - f (x ^ {*}) \leq \frac {4 L}{\sigma k ^ {2} c} C (x ^ {*}, x ^ {0}) = O \left(\frac {1}{k ^ {2}}\right),
items.statement:
Let $\{x^k\}, \{y^k\}$ be the sequences generated by IGA and let $x^*$ be an optimal solution of (P). Then for any $k \geq 0$ we have

$$
f (x ^ {k}) - f (x ^ {*}) \leq \frac {4 L}{\sigma k ^ {2} c} C (x ^ {*}, x ^ {0}) = O \left(\frac {1}{k ^ {2}}\right),
$$

where $C(x^{*},x^{0}) = c_{0}H(x^{*},x^{0}) + f(x^{0}) - f(x^{*})$ and the sequence $\{x^k\}$ is minimizing, i.e., $f(x^{k})\to f(x^{*})$.

items.latex: A \colon H \Rightarrow H ; B \colon H \Rightarrow H ; \operatorname{dom} A = H
items.statement: Assume that $A \colon H \Rightarrow H$ and $B \colon H \Rightarrow H$ are maximal monotone operators satisfying respectively $\operatorname{dom} A = H$ and $\operatorname{dom} B \neq \emptyset$. Given $x_0, x_1 \in H$ and a sequence $(\lambda_n)$ of positive numbers, the sequence $(x_n)$ is uniquely defined by the algorithm $(\mathcal{A})$ and the initial data $x_0, x_1$.
formulas: \Phi_ {A} (x) := \inf _ {y \in A (x)} \langle y, x \rangle .

items.name: Lemma 2.1
items.latex: A: H \Rightarrow H ; \operatorname{dom} A = H ; \forall x\in H,\Phi_A(x)\geqslant \sigma_{A(0)}(x)\geqslant 0.
items.statement:
Let $A: H \Rightarrow H$ be a monotone operator such that $\operatorname{dom} A = H$ and $0 \in A(0)$. The function $\Phi_A$ defined by (3) satisfies:

(i) $\forall x\in H,\Phi_A(x)\geqslant \sigma_{A(0)}(x)\geqslant 0.$  
(ii) $0 \in \operatorname{int}(A(0)) \Rightarrow \exists \alpha > 0, \quad \forall x \in H, \Phi_A(x) \geqslant \alpha |x|$ .
formulas:
\Phi_ {A} (x) := \inf _ {y \in A (x)} \langle y, x \rangle \geqslant \sup _ {z \in A (0)} \langle z, x \rangle = \sigma_ {A (0)} (x).
$$

On the other hand, since $0 \in A(0)$, it is clear that $\sigma_{A(0)}(x) \geqslant 0$.

(ii) According to a classical result, the assertion $0 \in \operatorname{int}(C)$ (where $C \subset H$ ) is equivalent to the existence of $\alpha > 0$ such that $\sigma_C \geqslant \alpha |\cdot|$. The conclusion is then an immediate consequence of (i).

Remark 2.1. In the particular case where $A := \partial g$, conclusion (i) of Lemma 2.1 can be slightly improved. Indeed, the subdifferential inequality yields:

$$
\forall x \in H, \quad \Phi_ {\partial g} (x) \geqslant g (x) - g (0) \geqslant \sigma_ {\partial g (0)} (x).

items.name: Proposition 2.2
items.latex: A \colon H \Rightarrow H ; \operatorname{dom} A = H ; f \colon H \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}
items.statement:
Let $A \colon H \Rightarrow H$ be a maximal monotone operator such that $\operatorname{dom} A = H$ and $0 \in A(0)$. The operator $B$ is supposed to be equal to $\partial f$ for a closed convex function $f \colon H \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ satisfying $\operatorname{dom} \partial f \neq \emptyset$ and $\inf f > -\infty$. The positive sequence $(\lambda_n)$ is assumed to be nondecreasing. Then, the sequence $(x_n)$ defined by algorithm $(\mathcal{A})$ satisfies:

(i) $E_{n + 1} - E_n \leqslant -\lambda_n \Phi_A((x_{n + 2} - x_{n + 1}) / \lambda_n)$, where the sequence $(E_n)$ and the function $\Phi_A$ are defined by (2) and (3), respectively.

(ii) $\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty}\lambda_n\Phi_A((x_{n+2}-x_{n+1})/\lambda_n) < +\infty.$
formulas:
\begin{aligned} E _ {n + 1} - E _ {n} &\leqslant \frac {1}{2 \lambda_ {n} ^ {2}} \left(\left| x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1} \right| ^ {2} - \left| x _ {n + 1} - x _ {n} \right| ^ {2}\right) + f (x _ {n + 2}) - f (x _ {n + 1}) \\ &\leqslant \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n} ^ {2}} \left\langle x _ {n + 2} - 2 x _ {n + 1} + x _ {n}, x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1} \right\rangle + f (x _ {n + 2}) - f (x _ {n + 1}). \\ \end{aligned}
$$

The convexity of $f$ gives $f(x_{n + 2}) - f(x_{n + 1}) \leqslant \langle v_{n + 2}, x_{n + 2} - x_{n + 1} \rangle$, so that the previous inequality yields

$$
E _ {n + 1} - E _ {n} \leqslant \big \langle (x _ {n + 2} - 2 x _ {n + 1} + x _ {n}) / \lambda_ {n} ^ {2} + v _ {n + 2}, x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1} \big \rangle .
$$

In view of inclusion (5) and the definition of $\Phi_A$, we immediately deduce

$$
E _ {n + 1} - E _ {n} \leqslant - \lambda_ {n} \Phi_ {A} ((x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1}) / \lambda_ {n}).

\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {N} \lambda_ {n} \Phi_ {A} ((x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1}) / \lambda_ {n}) \leqslant E _ {0} - E _ {N + 1} \leqslant E _ {0} - \inf f.
$$

Taking the limit when $N \rightarrow +\infty$ gives the expected conclusion.

Let us now apply the result of Proposition 2.2 to the case $A := \partial|\cdot|^{\alpha}$, for some $\alpha \geqslant 1$. In the sequel, $l^{\alpha}$ denotes the set of nonnegative sequences $(a_{n})$ satisfying $\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} a_{n}^{\alpha} < +\infty$.

COROLLARY 2.1. Let $f: H \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ be a closed convex function satisfying $\operatorname{dom} \partial f \neq 0$ and $\inf f > -\infty$. The operators $A$ and $B$ are supposed to be respectively defined by $A := \partial |\cdot|^{\alpha} (\alpha \geqslant 1)$ and $B := \partial f$. Consider a non decreasing sequence $(\lambda_n)$ of positive steps. Then, the sequence $(x_n)$ defined by $(\mathcal{A})$ satisfies $|(x_{n+2} - x_{n+1}) / \lambda_n| \in l^\alpha$.

Proof. From Proposition 2.2(ii) and expression (4), we obtain

$$
\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {+ \infty} \lambda_ {n} | (x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1}) / \lambda_ {n} | ^ {\alpha} <   + \infty .
$$

The conclusion follows from the fact that $\lambda_{n} \geqslant \lambda_{0} > 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

The case $\alpha = 1$ is specially interesting in the sense that $(|x_{n + 1} - x_n|) \in l^1$ implies the strong convergence of the sequence $(x_n)$. This remark is exploited in the next section, giving rise to a capital result of the paper.

# 3. Dry Friction Condition: $0 \in \operatorname{int}(A(0))$

In what follows, we will suppose that $0 \in \operatorname{int}(A(0))$. From the mechanical point of view, the assumption $0 \in \operatorname{int}(A(0))$ can be interpreted as a condition of dry friction. Examples of nonlinear oscillators subject to such a friction are given in [2, 7]. The fundamental aspect of the condition $0 \in \operatorname{int}(A(0))$ is the finite convergence of the associate algorithm $(\mathcal{A})$. According to the classical terminology, a sequence is said to be finitely convergent if it converges in a finite number of iterations. The question of finite convergence for proximal-like algorithms has given rise to an abundant literature (see for example [10-13]). Let us recall that the function $f: H \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ is linearly conditioned if $\arg\min f \neq \emptyset$ and there exists $\gamma > 0$ such that

$$
\forall x \in H, \quad f (x) \geqslant \min f + \gamma d (x, \operatorname{argmin} f)
$$

It is well known that the standard proximal method is finitely convergent for linearly conditioned convex functions. Our result does not require this kind of assumption. Here, the finite convergence of $(\mathcal{A})$ toward $x_{\infty}$, is obtained under a mild condition on $x_{\infty}$. This result is strongly related to the fact that oscillators subject to dry friction are stabilized in a finite time. We refer the reader to [1] where a continuous version of $(\mathcal{A})$ is studied in the particular case $A = \partial\Phi$ and $B = \nabla f$ (with $\Phi, f: H \to R$ respectively convex and differentiable).

In the following statement, we denote by $\mathcal{D}$ the set $\{n\in\mathbb{N},x_{n+1}=x_n\}$, where $(x_{n})$ is the sequence defined by algorithm $(\mathcal{A})$.

THEOREM 3.1. Let $A: H \Rightarrow H$ be a maximal monotone operator such that $\text{dom } A = H$ and $0 \in \text{int} (A(0))$. The operator $B$ is supposed to be equal to $\partial f$ for a closed convex function $f: H \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ satisfying $\text{dom } \partial f \neq \emptyset$ and $\inf f > -\infty$. The positive sequence $(\lambda_n)$ is assumed to be nondecreasing. Then, the sequence $(x_n)$ defined by algorithm $(\mathcal{A})$ satisfies:

(i) $(|x_{n+1} - x_n|) \in l^1$ and therefore $x_\infty := s - \lim_{n \to +\infty} x_n$ exists.  
(ii) The vector $x_{\infty}$ is such that $0 \in A(0) + \partial f(x_{\infty})$.  
(iii) If $H$ is finite-dimensional, then either the sequence $(x_{n})$ is finitely convergent or the limit points of $\left(\frac{x_{n+1} - x_n}{|x_{n+1} - x_n|}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathcal{D}}$ are contained in

$$
N _ {A (0)} (- \partial f (x _ {\infty})) := \bigcup_ {\xi \in - \partial f (x _ {\infty})} N _ {A (0)} (\xi).
$$

If moreover $-\partial f(x_{\infty}) \subset \operatorname{int}(A(0))$, the sequence $(x_n)$ is finitely convergent.

Proof. (i) From Lemma 2.1 (ii), the assumption $0 \in \operatorname{int}(A(0))$ implies that $\Phi_A \geqslant \alpha|\cdot|$. for some $\alpha > 0$. Assertion (i) is then an immediate consequence of Proposition 2.2.

(ii) Let $v_{n+2} \in \partial f(x_{n+2})$ satisfy:

$$
\left. - (x _ {n + 2} - 2 x _ {n + 1} + x _ {n}) / \lambda_ {n} ^ {2} - v _ {n + 2} \in A ((x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1}) / \lambda_ {n}). \right.

items.name: Corollary 2.1
items.statement: Let $f: H \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ be a closed convex function satisfying $\operatorname{dom} \partial f \neq 0$ and $\inf f > -\infty$. The operators $A$ and $B$ are supposed to be respectively defined by $A := \partial |\cdot|^{\alpha} (\alpha \geqslant 1)$ and $B := \partial f$. Consider a non decreasing sequence $(\lambda_n)$ of positive steps. Then, the sequence $(x_n)$ defined by $(\mathcal{A})$ satisfies $|(x_{n+2} - x_{n+1}) / \lambda_n| \in l^\alpha$.

items.name: Theorem 3.1
items.statement:
Let $A: H \Rightarrow H$ be a maximal monotone operator such that $\text{dom } A = H$ and $0 \in \text{int} (A(0))$. The operator $B$ is supposed to be equal to $\partial f$ for a closed convex function $f: H \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ satisfying $\text{dom } \partial f \neq \emptyset$ and $\inf f > -\infty$. The positive sequence $(\lambda_n)$ is assumed to be nondecreasing. Then, the sequence $(x_n)$ defined by algorithm $(\mathcal{A})$ satisfies:

(i) $(|x_{n+1} - x_n|) \in l^1$ and therefore $x_\infty := s - \lim_{n \to +\infty} x_n$ exists.  
(ii) The vector $x_{\infty}$ is such that $0 \in A(0) + \partial f(x_{\infty})$.  
(iii) If $H$ is finite-dimensional, then either the sequence $(x_{n})$ is finitely convergent or the limit points of $\left(\frac{x_{n+1} - x_n}{|x_{n+1} - x_n|}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathcal{D}}$ are contained in

$$
N _ {A (0)} (- \partial f (x _ {\infty})) := \bigcup_ {\xi \in - \partial f (x _ {\infty})} N _ {A (0)} (\xi).
$$

If moreover $-\partial f(x_{\infty}) \subset \operatorname{int}(A(0))$, the sequence $(x_n)$ is finitely convergent.
formulas:
\left\langle - (x _ {n + 2} - 2 x _ {n + 1} + x _ {n}) \Big / \lambda_ {n} ^ {2} - v _ {n + 2} - \xi , \frac {x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1}}{\left| x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1} \right|} \right\rangle \geqslant 0.
$$

By taking the limit in the previous inequality when $n \to +\infty$, we obtain $\langle -\overline{v} - \xi, d \rangle \geqslant 0$, which expresses that $d \in N_{A(0)}(-\overline{v}) \subset N_{A(0)}(-\partial f(x_{\infty}))$. Let us now assume that $-\partial f(x_{\infty}) \subset \operatorname{int}(A(0))$ and let us prove that the sequence $(x_n)$ is finitely convergent. We argue by contradiction and we still denote by $\overline{\omega}$ the set of limit points of $\left(\frac{x_{n+1} - x_n}{|x_{n+1} - x_n|}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N} \setminus \mathcal{D}}$. In view of $-\partial f(x_{\infty}) \subset \operatorname{int}(A(0))$, we have $\overline{\omega} \subset N_{A(0)}(-\partial f(x_{\infty})) = \{0\}$. Hence 0 is the unique limit point of the bounded sequence $\left(\frac{x_{n+1} - x_n}{|x_{n+1} - x_n|}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N} \setminus \mathcal{D}}$ and we conclude that $\lim_{n \to +\infty} \frac{x_{n+1} - x_n}{|x_{n+1} - x_n|} = 0$. This clearly contradicts the fact that $\frac{x_{n+1} - x_n}{|x_{n+1} - x_n|} \in \mathbb{S}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let us illustrate Theorem 3.1 by a few one-dimensional examples.

EXAMPLE 3.1. Take $H = \mathbb{R}$ and define the mappings $A$ and $f$ respectively by $A(x) = a \operatorname{sgn}(x)$ and $f(x) = bx^2 / 2$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive coefficients. The limit $x_{\infty}$ must fulfil the inclusion $0 \in a[-1, 1] + b x_{\infty}$, or equivalently $x_{\infty} \in [-a / b, a / b]$. If, moreover, $x_{\infty} \in ] -a / b, a / b[$, Theorem 3.1 (iii) asserts that the sequence $(x_n)$ finitely converges to $x_{\infty}$.

EXAMPLE 3.2. Take $H = \mathbb{R}$ and define the mappings $A$ and $f$ respectively by $A(x) = a \operatorname{sgn}(x)$ and $f(x) = b |x|$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive coefficients. The condition $0 \in A(0) + \partial f(x_{\infty})$ can be rewritten as: $0 \in a[-1, 1] + b \operatorname{sgn}(x_{\infty})$. If $b > a$, the unique solution of the previous inclusion is $x_{\infty} = 0$ so that the sequence $(x_n)$ converges toward 0. Now assume that $b \leqslant a$. It is then elementary to check that every $x_{\infty} \in \mathbb{R}$ is solution of $0 \in A(0) + \partial f(x_{\infty})$ : the sequence $(x_n)$ may converge toward any element of $\mathbb{R}$. If, moreover, $b < a$, the convergence is finite.

Let us give a counterexample to finite convergence when $-\partial f(x_{\infty}) \not\subset \text{int}(A(0))$.

EXAMPLE 3.3. Take $H = \mathbb{R}$ and define the operator $A$ (resp. the function $f$ ) by $A(x) = \operatorname{sgn}(x) + 2x$ (resp. $f(x) = x^2 / 2$ ). If the sequence $(\lambda_n)$ is constant and equal to 1, the algorithm $(\mathcal{A})$ reduces to

$$
x _ {n + 2} - 2 x _ {n + 1} + x _ {n} + \operatorname{sgn} \left(x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1}\right) + 2 (x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1}) + x _ {n + 2} \ni 0,
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
4 x _ {n + 2} - 4 x _ {n + 1} + x _ {n} \in - \mathrm{sgn} (x _ {n + 2} - x _ {n + 1}).
$$

Take as initial data $x_0 = x_1 = 2$. We let the reader check that the expression of $x_n$ is given by $x_n = 1 + (1 + n)/2^n$, so that $(x_n)$ converges toward $x_\infty := 1$. There is no finite convergence but simply geometrical convergence, because of $-1 = -f'(1) \notin \operatorname{int}(A(0)) = ] - 1, 1[$.

In the next sections, we will focus on the particular case where the function $f$ is smooth. In this situation, Theorem 3.1 shows that finite convergence holds as soon as $-\nabla f(x_{\infty}) \notin \mathrm{bd}(A(0))$. Since the boundary of the convex set $A(0)$ has an empty interior, it is reasonable to think that the circumstances leading to $-\nabla f(x_{\infty}) \in \mathrm{bd}(A(0))$ are 'exceptional'. The purpose of the next two sections is to precise the asymptotic properties of $(\mathcal{A})$ in this case, which will be referred to as the 'boundary case'. The corresponding study for the continuous dynamical system $(S)$ has been performed by the second author in the recent paper [8].

# 4. Analysis of the Boundary Case (I): A(0) Smooth

Throughout this section, we assume that $H$ is finite-dimensional. Let us recall that a convex set $C \subset H$ is said to be smooth at a point $\overline{x} \in C$ if $N_C(\overline{x})$ is reduced to a half-line. The set $C$ is said to be smooth if it is smooth at every point of its boundary.
